short: A buying frenzy in the 1630s Dutch Republic when prices of rare tulip bulbs soared, then collapsed in February 1637.
kid: Long ago, people in one country decided special flower bulbs were super precious. They paid more and more for them, until one day nobody wanted to buy, and the bulbs were just bulbs again.
detail: Tulip mania was a burst of speculation in the Dutch Republic that peaked in the winter of 1636-37. Rare 'broken' tulips with flamed petals, a pattern later traced to a plant virus, became status symbols. Traders meeting in taverns signed contracts to buy bulbs still in the ground for delivery the next spring, an early form of futures trading. Prices of some varieties multiplied within weeks, then collapsed in early February 1637 when buyers stopped turning up at auctions in Haarlem. Many contracts were never honoured, and buyers were eventually allowed to settle for a small fraction. It is the classic story of a bubble: prices driven by expected resale rather than real use. The common confusion: historians now find the wider Dutch economy barely suffered, so the popular tale of mass ruin is exaggerated.
example: Say a trader agreed in January 1637 to pay 1,000 guilders in spring for a bulb, and by February similar bulbs fetched 100 guilders. Honouring the deal meant paying 900 guilders more than the bulb was worth. In Haarlem, buyers were later allowed to cancel such contracts by paying 3.5% of the agreed price, here 35 guilders.

short: The 1720 boom and crash in shares of Britain's South Sea Company, which had swapped government debt for its own stock.
kid: A company told everyone it would bring back treasure from faraway seas. Lots of people rushed to own a piece of it, but the treasure never really came, and most of them lost what they paid.
detail: The South Sea Company was set up in 1711 with a monopoly on British trade with Spanish South America, though war and Spanish limits meant little real trade. Its real business was government finance: in 1720 it offered to take over much of Britain's national debt, letting holders swap their government debt for South Sea shares. The higher the share price, the fewer shares it had to hand each debt holder, so insiders talked the price up, helped by bribes to politicians and company loans to buy its own shares. The stock went from about £128 in January 1720 to around £1,000 by summer, then collapsed to about £150 by late September. Isaac Newton reportedly lost heavily. It is a lesson in bubbles built on a story rather than profits. Do not confuse it with France's Mississippi Bubble of the same year.
example: An investor who bought 10 shares at about £1,000 each in the summer of 1720 paid £10,000. At about £150 a share in late September, the holding was worth £1,500, a loss of 85%.

short: A money system in which a currency is defined as a fixed weight of gold and can be swapped for gold at that price.
kid: Imagine every paper ticket you hold can be swapped for a tiny piece of shiny gold kept in a big safe. Nobody can make more tickets unless they have more gold.
detail: Under a gold standard the government fixes its currency's price in gold and promises to convert notes into gold on demand. Because each currency is tied to gold, exchange rates between gold-standard countries are effectively fixed. The classical gold standard ran roughly from the 1870s to 1914; a weaker version returned in the 1920s and broke down in the Great Depression, with Britain leaving in 1931 and the US devaluing in 1933-34. Bretton Woods kept a link through the US dollar until 1971. Gold limits money printing and inflation, but it also ties a central bank's hands in a crisis: countries that left gold earlier generally recovered from the Depression faster. India's rupee was on silver until the 1890s and later linked to gold only indirectly, through sterling. No major currency is gold-backed today; a central bank holding gold reserves is a different thing.
example: The US fixed gold at $20.67 an ounce until 1933. In January 1934 it reset the price to $35, so the dollar price of gold rose about 69% (14.33 / 20.67), and each dollar now bought about 41% less gold (1 − 20.67 / 35).
formula: Mint parity (units of currency A per unit of currency B) = Official gold price in currency A / Official gold price in currency B

short: The collapse of US share prices in October 1929, the start of a slide that wiped out almost 90% of the Dow's value by 1932.
kid: Lots of grown-ups had been buying little pieces of big companies with borrowed pocket money, sure those pieces would keep getting more precious. Then everyone got scared at once, rushed to sell, and the values tumbled.
detail: The crash ended a 1920s boom in which the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose about sixfold from its 1921 low, much of it fuelled by investors buying on margin, often putting down only 10% to 20% and borrowing the rest from brokers. After peaking at 381.17 on 3 September 1929, prices wobbled, then broke: Black Thursday (24 October) brought panic selling, and Black Monday and Black Tuesday (28 and 29 October) cut the Dow by about 13% and 12%. Margin calls forced still more selling. The slide continued until July 1932, when the Dow hit 41.22, and it did not regain its 1929 peak until 1954. The common confusion is that the crash alone caused the Great Depression; bank failures, a shrinking money supply and policy mistakes did more damage. It led to the creation of the SEC and to tighter margin rules.
example: The Dow fell from 381.17 in September 1929 to 41.22 in July 1932, a drop of about 89% (339.95 / 381.17). An investor who put down $1,000 and borrowed $9,000 to buy $10,000 of shares was wiped out by the first 10% fall.

short: The severe worldwide economic slump of the 1930s, marked by collapsing output, mass unemployment, falling prices and waves of bank failures.
kid: For a long time, many grown-ups could not find work, shops sold less and less, and families had very little. It took years, and lots of help, for things to get better.
detail: The Great Depression began in 1929 and lasted, in most countries, until the late 1930s. In the US, real output fell by about a quarter between 1929 and 1933, unemployment reached about 25%, prices fell by roughly a quarter and around 9,000 banks failed. As banks collapsed, the money supply shrank by about a third, and falling prices made debts heavier in real terms. The gold standard spread the slump between countries and stopped central banks from easing, while tariffs such as the US Smoot-Hawley Act of 1930 choked trade. India was hit through collapsing crop prices, which squeezed farmers and pushed households to sell gold. The Depression created many modern tools: deposit insurance, securities regulators and active fiscal and monetary policy. Do not confuse a depression with an ordinary recession; it is far deeper and lasts far longer.
example: Say a farmer owed $1,000 and wheat sold at $1 a bushel, so repaying took 1,000 bushels. If wheat fell to 50 cents, the same debt took 2,000 bushels. US unemployment rose from about 3% in 1929 to about 25% in 1933.

short: The runaway inflation in Germany in 1921-23, when prices rose so fast that the paper mark became almost worthless by November 1923.
kid: Imagine a sweet costs one coin today, ten coins next week and a whole wheelbarrow of paper notes next month. The paper notes became so useless that some people burned them to keep warm.
detail: After the First World War, Germany's Weimar Republic faced heavy war debts and reparation payments under the Treaty of Versailles, and it covered its deficits by having the Reichsbank print money. When France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr industrial region in January 1923 and Germany paid striking workers with freshly printed marks, inflation exploded: by late 1923 prices were doubling every few days. A dollar that bought 4.2 marks in 1914 bought about 4.2 trillion marks by November 1923, wiping out savings and anyone holding fixed-income investments. It ended with a new currency, the Rentenmark, worth one trillion old marks, plus budget cuts and the 1924 Dawes Plan. It is the textbook case for central bank independence. Do not confuse it with ordinary high inflation: hyperinflation is usually defined as prices rising more than 50% a month.
example: In 1914 one US dollar bought 4.2 marks; by November 1923 it bought about 4.2 trillion, a trillion-fold collapse. Even the 50% monthly threshold compounds brutally: 1.5 raised to the 12th power is about 129.7, so prices rise roughly 12,875% in a year.

short: The post-1944 world currency system: currencies were pegged to the US dollar, which foreign central banks could swap for gold at $35 an ounce.
kid: After a big war, many countries agreed to keep their play tickets worth a set number of one big friend's tickets. That friend promised to swap his tickets for gold, so everyone felt safe swapping.
detail: In July 1944, delegates from 44 Allied countries, India among them, met at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, to design a stable post-war monetary order. Each country set a par value for its currency against the US dollar and kept it within 1% either side, while the US promised foreign central banks it would convert dollars into gold at $35 an ounce. Pegs could be changed only to fix a 'fundamental disequilibrium', and capital controls were allowed. The conference also created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, still called the Bretton Woods institutions. The system strained as US gold fell short of foreign dollar holdings and ended with the Nixon shock of 1971; by 1973 major currencies floated. The common confusion: the exchange-rate system died, but the institutions live on. India's 1966 devaluation happened under these rules.
example: Under Bretton Woods India's par value was ₹4.76 per dollar from 1949, so the rupee had to stay between about ₹4.71 and ₹4.81 (1% either side). In June 1966 the par value moved to ₹7.50, so a $1,000 import bill rose from ₹4,760 to ₹7,500, about 58% more.

short: The Indian government's takeover of 14 large private banks on 19 July 1969, to steer bank lending towards farmers, small businesses and rural India.
kid: Fourteen big piggy-bank keepers used to be run by a few rich families. The government took them over so they would also look after farmers and people in small villages.
detail: On 19 July 1969, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's government nationalised the 14 commercial banks that each held deposits of ₹50 crore or more, together about 85% of the country's deposits. The aim was to end 'class banking', in which big business houses got most loans, and to push credit and branches into villages. The Supreme Court struck down the first law in 1970, so it was re-enacted, and six more banks were nationalised in 1980. Branches multiplied, rural savings were mobilised and priority sector lending targets for agriculture and small industry followed. The costs were political lending, weak efficiency and recurring bad loans, which the post-1991 reforms and later recapitalisations tried to fix. Today's public sector banks descend from this move. Common confusion: State Bank of India was not part of 1969; it was created in 1955 from the Imperial Bank of India.
example: The 1969 step took over 14 banks and 1980 added six more, making 20 nationalised banks at the time. Under the priority sector rules that grew from it, a domestic commercial bank with, say, ₹10,000 crore of adjusted net bank credit must lend at least 40%, or ₹4,000 crore, to sectors such as agriculture and small firms, under RBI rules as of 2025.

short: US President Nixon's decision on 15 August 1971 to stop swapping dollars for gold, which ended the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates.
kid: A friend had always promised to swap his tickets for shiny gold whenever you asked. One day he said no more swapping, and after that his tickets were worth whatever people agreed they were.
detail: By the late 1960s foreign governments held far more dollars than the US had gold to honour at $35 an ounce, thanks to US deficits, Vietnam War spending and rising inflation. On 15 August 1971, President Richard Nixon suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold for foreign central banks, imposed a 10% surcharge on imports and froze wages and prices for 90 days. The December 1971 Smithsonian Agreement tried to rescue fixed rates with a devalued dollar and gold at $38, but by March 1973 the major currencies were floating. The shock began today's era of fiat money, backed by trust in central banks rather than metal. Floating exchange rates, a free gold price and modern currency markets all date from it. The common confusion: Americans had already been barred from holding monetary gold since 1933, so the 1971 move affected foreign governments.
example: The official gold price went from $35 to $38 an ounce in December 1971, a rise of about 8.6% (3 / 35), and to $42.22 in February 1973, about 11.1% more (4.22 / 38). Once gold traded freely, its market price reached about $850 in January 1980, roughly 24 times the old $35 peg.

short: The 1973-74 cut-off of oil sales by Arab producers that roughly quadrupled crude prices and pushed rich economies into recession with high inflation.
kid: Some countries that had lots of fuel for cars suddenly sold much less of it. Cars waited in long lines to fill up, and lots of things cost more because almost everything needs fuel to move.
detail: In October 1973, during the Yom Kippur War, Arab members of OPEC cut output and banned oil sales to the United States, the Netherlands and other supporters of Israel. The posted price of benchmark Saudi crude rose from about $3 a barrel to $11.65 by January 1974. The embargo ended in March 1974, but prices stayed high, and a second shock followed the 1979 Iranian revolution. Oil importers suffered stagflation: stagnant output and rising unemployment alongside high inflation, which undercut the belief that inflation and unemployment could not both be high at once. Exporters' surplus petrodollars were recycled through Western banks as loans to developing countries, sowing the 1980s debt crisis. India's import bill jumped, straining its balance of payments. The confusion to avoid: the embargo itself was short; the lasting damage came from the permanently higher price and the inflation it fed.
example: The posted price of Saudi Arabian Light crude rose from $3.01 a barrel in early October 1973 to $11.65 in January 1974, nearly four times as much. For a country importing 100 million barrels a year, the bill would jump from $301 million to $1,165 million.

short: The US Federal Reserve's sharp interest-rate increases under Paul Volcker from 1979, which crushed double-digit inflation at the cost of deep recessions.
kid: Things in the shops kept getting dearer every week, so the grown-up in charge made borrowing very hard for a while. People bought less and it hurt, but the price tags finally stopped jumping up.
detail: By 1979 US inflation was above 11% and people expected more. Paul Volcker became Fed chair in August 1979 and on 6 October switched the Fed to controlling the growth of bank reserves, letting short-term interest rates go wherever needed. The federal funds rate swung wildly and averaged about 19% in mid-1981; banks' prime lending rate touched 21.5%. The economy fell into back-to-back recessions in 1980 and 1981-82, unemployment reached 10.8%, and high US rates helped trigger the Latin American debt crisis. But consumer inflation fell from a peak of 14.8% in March 1980 to around 3% by 1983, and the Fed won credibility that anchored expectations for decades. Investors still invoke it when asking whether a central bank will accept pain to beat inflation. Do not confuse it with the Volcker Rule, the 2010 curb on banks' proprietary trading.
example: In mid-1981 the federal funds rate averaged about 19% while consumer inflation ran near 10%, a real interest rate of roughly 9%. A business borrowing $1 million for a year at 19% owed about $190,000 in interest, which is why investment and hiring collapsed.
formula: Real interest rate ≈ Nominal interest rate − Inflation rate

short: A 1985 agreement by five major economies to push the overvalued US dollar down, mainly against the Japanese yen and German mark.
kid: Five friends agreed that one friend's stickers had become too pricey to swap. So they all worked together to make his stickers a bit less precious, which made everyone else's stickers worth more.
detail: On 22 September 1985 the finance ministers and central bank governors of the G5 (the US, Japan, West Germany, France and the UK) met at New York's Plaza Hotel and agreed to intervene jointly in currency markets to weaken the dollar. A strong dollar, driven by high US interest rates, had swollen the US trade deficit and fuelled protectionist pressure in Congress. The dollar, already slipping, then fell steeply, roughly halving against the yen within about two years. In February 1987 the G6, meeting at the Louvre in Paris, agreed the fall had gone far enough and tried to stabilise it. The yen's surge hurt Japanese exporters, and the Bank of Japan's easy-money response helped inflate Japan's late-1980s bubble. Whenever the dollar looks overvalued, markets debate a 'new Plaza Accord'. The common confusion: intervention worked partly because policy and sentiment were already shifting.
example: The dollar bought about 240 yen just before the Plaza meeting and about 120 by the end of 1987. A Japanese carmaker selling a $10,000 car in the US earned about 2.4 million yen before and about 1.2 million yen after, so it had to raise its dollar price or accept half the yen revenue.

short: The stock market crash of 19 October 1987, when the Dow Jones fell 22.6% in one day, its largest one-day percentage fall ever.
kid: One Monday, almost everyone wanted to sell their pieces of companies at the same moment, and hardly anyone wanted to buy. The values dropped a lot in a single day, then slowly climbed back over the next two years.
detail: On Black Monday, 19 October 1987, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 508 points, or 22.6%, and markets from Hong Kong to London crashed alongside it. Stocks had risen strongly that year, and worries about rising interest rates, the US trade deficit and a weak dollar had been building. Mechanical selling made it worse: portfolio insurance strategies sold stock index futures as prices fell, and computer-driven program trading swamped market makers. The Fed, under new chair Alan Greenspan, promised liquidity the next morning, which helped stop the panic and is often seen as the start of the 'Fed put' idea. There was no recession, and the Dow regained its pre-crash high by 1989. The crash led to circuit breakers that pause trading after big falls. Do not confuse it with the many other 'black Mondays' headlines use for any sharp fall.
example: The Dow closed at 2,246.74 on Friday 16 October 1987 and at 1,738.74 on Monday 19 October, a fall of 508 points, or 22.6% (508 / 2,246.74). A $10,000 holding that tracked the index would have been worth about $7,739 by the close.

short: Japan's long stretch of weak growth and falling prices after its stock market and property bubble burst around 1990.
kid: A family spent a lot on toys, sure they would keep getting more valuable. When that stopped, they spent years paying back and saving, so the house stayed quiet and nothing grew much.
detail: In the late 1980s, cheap credit and soaring optimism inflated a giant bubble in Japanese shares and land; at the peak, the land under Tokyo's Imperial Palace was said to be worth more than all of California. The Nikkei 225 peaked at 38,915.87 on 29 December 1989. Bank of Japan rate rises, begun in May 1989, burst the bubble, and stock and land prices fell for years. Banks sat on bad loans and kept weak 'zombie' borrowers alive, companies used cash to pay down debt instead of investing, and prices began falling in the late 1990s. The 1990s became the 'lost decade', later stretched to 'lost decades'. Japan pioneered zero rates and quantitative easing in response, and later adopted negative rates. Investors use 'Japanification' as shorthand for low growth, low inflation and low yields. The common confusion: Japan stayed rich and stable; what it lost was growth, not prosperity.
example: The Nikkei 225 fell from 38,915.87 at the end of 1989 to 7,054.98 in March 2009, a decline of about 82% (1 − 7,054.98 / 38,915.87). It did not close above its 1989 record until February 2024, more than 34 years later.

short: India's 1991 emergency when its foreign currency reserves fell to a few weeks of imports, forcing it to pledge gold and borrow from the IMF.
kid: Our country needed to buy things from other countries, but its jar of foreign coins was almost empty. So it handed over some gold as a promise, borrowed help, and then changed many of its rules.
detail: Through the 1980s India ran large government deficits and a widening current account deficit, financed more and more by short-term foreign borrowing and deposits from non-resident Indians. In 1990-91 the Gulf crisis pushed up oil prices and cut remittances from workers in Kuwait, while political instability and credit-rating downgrades made lenders pull back. By mid-1991 foreign exchange reserves covered barely a few weeks of imports, and default on external debt loomed. The government moved fast: about 20 tonnes of gold were sold with an option to buy back, and in July 1991 the RBI pledged about 47 tonnes with the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan to raise roughly $400 million. The rupee was devalued by about 18-19% in two steps, IMF loans were arranged and sweeping reforms followed. The common confusion: India never defaulted; it was a liquidity crisis, not bankruptcy.
example: Say reserves are $1.2 billion and imports run at $2 billion a month. Import cover is then 0.6 months (1.2 / 2), or about 18 days, which is roughly where India stood in mid-1991.
formula: Import cover (months) = Foreign exchange reserves / Average monthly imports

short: The changes India began in July 1991 that scrapped most industrial licences, cut import duties, opened the door to foreign investment and freed up markets.
kid: For a long time, you needed a special permission slip to open a new shop or bring toys from abroad. In 1991 most of those slips were torn up, so more people could make, sell and trade things.
detail: Prompted by the 1991 balance of payments crisis, Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh launched reforms often summed up as LPG: liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation. The New Industrial Policy of 24 July 1991 abolished industrial licensing for all but a short list of industries, removed curbs on big business houses and allowed automatic approval of foreign investment up to 51% in priority sectors. Import duties, once among the world's highest, were cut steadily, the rupee was devalued and then moved to a market-based rate, and the current account became convertible in 1994. Financial reforms followed: statutory powers for SEBI, new private banks, screen-based trading on the NSE and lower reserve requirements for banks. Growth picked up markedly in the following decades. The common confusion: 1991 was the decisive break, but reform was gradual and some steps began in the 1980s.
example: Say ABC Ltd imports a machine worth ₹10 lakh. At a 150% import duty its landed cost is ₹25 lakh; if the duty falls to 50%, the cost drops to ₹15 lakh, making the machine 40% cheaper. Cuts of this kind through the 1990s made Indian factories cheaper to equip and more competitive.

short: The 1992 fraud in which broker Harshad Mehta diverted bank money meant for government bond deals into shares, fuelling a stock market boom.
kid: A clever trader borrowed huge piles of coins from the town's safe-keepers using promise notes with nothing behind them. He used the coins to push up company prices, and when the trick was discovered, it all came crashing down.
detail: In the early 1990s, Indian banks traded government securities with each other through 'ready forward' deals, a form of repo, often arranged by brokers and settled with paper bank receipts instead of actual transfer of securities. Harshad Mehta, a Mumbai broker, exploited weak controls: cheques meant for one bank were routed through his account, and unbacked bank receipts from small banks covered the gaps. The money, estimated at around ₹4,000 crore, flowed into shares, and the Sensex more than tripled in about a year to roughly 4,500 in April 1992. When journalist Sucheta Dalal exposed the scheme that month, the market crashed and several banks were left with huge losses. The scandal sped up reforms: a stronger SEBI, the screen-based NSE, depositories and tighter RBI rules on bank trading. The common confusion: it was mainly a banking-system fraud, not just stock manipulation.
example: Say a broker borrowed ₹100 crore through such a deal for 15 days at 15% a year. The interest would be ₹100 crore × 15% × 15/365, about ₹61.6 lakh, so the shares bought had to rise more than about 0.62% in a fortnight for the bet to pay; when prices fell, the losses landed on the lending bank.

short: The 1997-98 currency and banking crisis that began when Thailand stopped defending the baht and spread across East Asia.
kid: Some neighbours borrowed lots of toys from far away and promised to give back the exact same toys later. When their own toys lost value, they had to hand over far more of them to pay back, and many got into big trouble.
detail: Through the early 1990s, fast-growing East Asian economies attracted heavy foreign lending while keeping their currencies roughly pegged to the dollar. Banks and companies borrowed short-term in dollars and lent or invested long-term in local currency, often in property. On 2 July 1997 Thailand, running out of reserves, let the baht float; it sank, and panic spread to Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia and the Philippines. Currencies collapsed, dollar debts became unpayable in local terms, and output shrank sharply in 1998. The IMF arranged large rescues for Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea, with tough conditions, while Malaysia imposed capital controls instead. Indonesia's crisis helped topple President Suharto. India was largely shielded by capital controls, low short-term foreign debt and limited foreign borrowing. The lesson for investors: currency mismatches, fixed pegs and hot money make a dangerous mix.
example: Say a Thai company borrowed $10 million when the baht was 25 to the dollar, a debt worth 250 million baht. When the baht fell to 50 per dollar, the same debt was worth 500 million baht: twice the burden, without borrowing a single extra dollar.

short: A giant US hedge fund, run by star traders and Nobel-winning economists, whose heavily borrowed bets failed in 1998 and threatened global markets.
kid: A team of very clever people made lots of tiny bets that looked almost sure to win, using mostly borrowed coins. When something surprising happened, all the bets went wrong together, and others had to rush in to help clean up.
detail: Long-Term Capital Management was founded in 1994 by former Salomon Brothers trader John Meriwether, with partners including Nobel laureates Myron Scholes and Robert Merton. It ran convergence trades: buying slightly cheaper bonds and selling similar, slightly dearer ones, betting the small price gap would close. Each gap was tiny, so LTCM used enormous leverage, with derivatives positions above $1 trillion in notional value. After stellar early returns, Russia's default in August 1998 sent investors fleeing to the safest, most liquid assets, and the gaps widened instead of closing. LTCM lost about $4.6 billion in a few months. Fearing fire sales across markets, the New York Fed brought 14 banks together to inject about $3.6 billion in September 1998; no public money was used. The lesson: models that assume normal markets underestimate fat tails, liquidity risk and crowded trades.
example: At the start of 1998 LTCM had about $4.7 billion of equity supporting about $129 billion of assets, leverage of roughly 27 times (129 / 4.7). At that level a fall of under 4% in asset values (4.7 / 129 is about 3.6%) would erase all of its capital.

short: The late-1990s boom in internet and technology shares that burst in 2000, wiping out most of the Nasdaq's value by 2002.
kid: Everyone got excited about a new invention and wanted a piece of any company that used it, even ones that had never sold much. When people realised many of those companies would never earn enough, the excitement popped like a balloon.
detail: As the internet spread in the late 1990s, investors poured money into almost any company with '.com' in its name, valuing them on website visits, 'eyeballs' and growth stories rather than profits. Easy funding and a wave of IPOs whose shares often doubled on day one fed the frenzy. The Nasdaq Composite, heavy with tech shares, peaked at 5,048.62 on 10 March 2000. As the Fed raised rates and cash-burning start-ups ran out of money, prices collapsed; many companies, like Pets.com, shut down, and even survivors such as Amazon fell more than 90%. India saw its own version in technology, media and telecom stocks around 2000. The common confusion: the internet itself was not a fad; the mistake was the price paid for it. Similar debates now surround new technologies such as artificial intelligence.
example: The Nasdaq Composite fell from 5,048.62 in March 2000 to 1,114.11 in October 2002, a loss of about 78%. $10,000 invested at the peak would have shrunk to about $2,207, and the index did not regain its 2000 high until 2015.

short: The 2001 Indian scandal in which broker Ketan Parekh used bank funds and coordinated trading to pump up favoured shares called the K-10 stocks.
kid: A trader and his friends kept passing a few toys back and forth to make them look super popular, so others paid a lot for them. He had borrowed to do it, and when the game stopped, the people who lent to him were left in trouble.
detail: During the 1999-2000 technology and media boom, Mumbai broker Ketan Parekh became the market's most powerful operator. He concentrated on a handful of stocks, dubbed the K-10, mostly technology, media and telecom names, and pushed them up through circular trading among related entities. Funds came from friendly companies, Global Trust Bank and especially Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank, which issued him pay orders without adequate backing. When prices fell after the 2000 tech bust and heavy selling around the February 2001 Budget, he could not meet his payments. The co-operative bank collapsed, the Calcutta Stock Exchange suffered a payment crisis, and SEBI later barred him from the market. Reforms followed: the badla carry-forward system was abolished, rolling settlement replaced weekly settlement and the RBI curbed bank lending to brokers. Do not confuse it with Harshad Mehta's 1992 scam, which drew money from the bank bond market.
example: Say related accounts trade 1 lakh shares of a thinly traded hypothetical XYZ Ltd back and forth, pushing the price from ₹100 to ₹400. The holding now looks worth ₹4 crore and can be pledged for loans; when the price falls back to ₹100 it is worth ₹1 crore, a 75% fall in the collateral behind those loans.

short: The 1998-2001 crisis at US-64, India's largest mutual fund scheme, when its promised buyback prices exceeded what its investments were really worth.
kid: A huge shared jar promised everyone they could always swap their tickets back for a fixed number of sweets. Inside there were fewer sweets than promised, so one day it had to say please wait, and the grown-ups in charge had to top it up.
detail: US-64, launched in 1964 by the government-backed Unit Trust of India, was the country's first and biggest mutual fund scheme, held by millions of small investors who treated it almost like a deposit. Unlike a normal mutual fund, UTI set its own sale and repurchase prices and paid steady dividends instead of pricing units at their net asset value (NAV). In the 1990s its equity bets soured, and by 1998 its NAV had fallen below the repurchase price, requiring a government rescue. Trouble returned after the 2000-01 market slump, including losses on stocks linked to the Ketan Parekh scam; in July 2001 UTI froze repurchases for six months, setting off public anger. In 2003 the government split UTI into the SEBI-regulated UTI Mutual Fund and a government-run Specified Undertaking. The lesson: a fund promising fixed exits must eventually face the true value of its assets.
example: Say a scheme promises to buy back units at ₹14 while the assets behind each unit are worth only ₹8. Every unit redeemed pays out ₹6 more than it is worth, so redeeming 1 crore units costs the remaining investors, or the government, ₹6 crore.
formula: NAV per unit = (Market value of assets − Liabilities) / Units outstanding

short: The 2001 collapse of US energy giant Enron after it was revealed to have hidden debts and inflated profits through accounting tricks.
kid: A big company drew a very pretty picture of how well it was doing and hid its problems in secret boxes. When people opened the boxes and saw the truth, the company fell apart almost overnight.
detail: Enron, a Houston energy and trading company, ranked seventh on the Fortune 500 in 2001 and was hailed as an innovator. Behind the image, executives used mark-to-market accounting to book estimated future profits upfront and parked losses and debt in off-balance-sheet special purpose entities, some run by finance chief Andrew Fastow. In October 2001 it reported a large loss and a $1.2 billion cut to shareholders' equity; on 2 December 2001 it filed for bankruptcy, then the largest in US history. Employees lost jobs and retirement savings held in Enron stock. Its auditor, Arthur Andersen, collapsed after a conviction for obstruction that was later overturned. The scandal produced the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 on internal controls and auditor independence. India knew Enron through the controversial Dabhol power project in Maharashtra. The lesson: reported profits mean little if cash flows and debts are hidden.
example: Enron's shares fell from a peak of about $90 in August 2000 to under $1 by late November 2001. An investor who put $10,000 in at the peak bought about 111 shares, which were worth less than $111 some fifteen months later.

short: The 2007 wave of US home-loan defaults by risky borrowers, which spread through mortgage-linked securities and triggered the 2008 global financial crisis.
kid: Lots of families were lent money for houses even when they would struggle to pay it back. When many could not pay at once, the people who had lent it, and everyone who had bought their promises, were in trouble too.
detail: In the early 2000s, low interest rates, rising house prices and loose standards led US lenders to make 'subprime' mortgages to borrowers with weak credit, often with low teaser rates that reset higher after two or three years and little proof of income. Lenders sold the loans to be packaged into mortgage-backed securities and CDOs, many rated AAA, which were sold to investors worldwide. As the Fed raised rates from 2004 and house prices peaked in 2006, rate resets and falling prices pushed defaults up, and borrowers could no longer refinance. In 2007 subprime lenders failed, two Bear Stearns hedge funds collapsed, and in August BNP Paribas froze funds it could not value, jamming interbank lending. The common confusion: subprime loans were a modest slice of US mortgages; the damage came from leverage, opaque securities and the loss of trust between banks.
example: Say a borrower takes a $200,000 interest-only loan at a 4% teaser rate, paying $8,000 a year. When the rate resets to 8%, the bill doubles to $16,000. If the house, bought for $250,000, falls 20% to $200,000, the owner's stake is gone and refinancing is impossible.

short: The 2007-09 meltdown of the global banking system, centred on US mortgage losses, that caused the deepest worldwide recession since the 1930s.
kid: Many big money-keepers had made risky promises to each other. When a few broke their promises, nobody trusted anyone, lending stopped, and lots of people around the world lost their jobs for a while.
detail: The crisis grew out of the US subprime mortgage bust, but the damage came from a leveraged, tightly linked financial system. Banks and shadow banks held mortgage securities financed with short-term borrowing; when their value became doubtful, lenders pulled back. Bear Stearns was rescued in March 2008. September 2008 brought panic: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac were taken over, Lehman Brothers went bankrupt, AIG was rescued and a money market fund broke the buck. Credit froze worldwide. Governments responded with bailouts such as TARP, deposit guarantees and stimulus; central banks slashed rates, opened swap lines and began quantitative easing. In India the Sensex lost over half its value, foreign money fled and the RBI cut the repo rate from 9% to 4.75% within months. Basel III, stress tests and Dodd-Frank followed. The Great Recession is the economic slump that came with it.
example: The S&P 500 fell from 1,565.15 in October 2007 to 676.53 in March 2009, a loss of about 57%. $10,000 in an index fund at the peak was worth about $4,322 at the bottom and needed a gain of about 131% just to get back to $10,000.

short: The 15 September 2008 bankruptcy of US investment bank Lehman Brothers, the largest in US history, which turned a banking scare into global panic.
kid: A very old and very big money-keeper had borrowed far too much to buy risky things. When nobody would lend to it any more and nobody saved it, it shut down, and everyone else got scared about who would be next.
detail: Lehman Brothers, founded in 1850, was the fourth-largest US investment bank, with heavy bets on property and mortgage securities funded by short-term borrowing at leverage of around 30 times. As losses mounted in 2008 it struggled to raise capital and used accounting moves such as 'Repo 105' to make its debt look smaller. Having already helped rescue Bear Stearns and taken over Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, US authorities refused to put public money into Lehman, and talks with Barclays and Bank of America failed. Lehman filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008 with about $639 billion in assets. Money market funds holding its paper suffered, banks stopped lending to each other and the crisis went global. Barclays bought its US business, and Nomura took its Asian and European arms, including operations in India. A 'Lehman moment' now means one failure that triggers system-wide panic.
example: At leverage of about 31 times, roughly where Lehman stood at the end of 2007, a bank holds $31 of assets for every $1 of equity, so a fall of just 3.2% in asset values (1 / 31) wipes out all its equity. That thin cushion is why falling mortgage values sank it so quickly.

short: The US government's $700 billion rescue fund created in October 2008 to stabilise banks, carmakers and the housing market during the financial crisis.
kid: When the biggest money-keepers were about to topple over, the government gave them a hand and some coins to stand up again. Later, most of them paid the coins back.
detail: The Troubled Asset Relief Program was created by the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act, signed on 3 October 2008 after the House first rejected it, a vote that sent the Dow down 778 points. It authorised up to $700 billion, later cut to $475 billion. The original idea was to buy toxic mortgage assets from banks, but pricing them proved too slow, so the Treasury instead injected capital directly by buying preferred shares and warrants in hundreds of banks, starting with $125 billion in nine of the largest. TARP also funded the rescue of AIG, the bailout of General Motors and Chrysler, and mortgage relief schemes. Most bank money was repaid with dividends, and the final net cost was a small fraction of the headline figure. It remains controversial for rescuing Wall Street while homeowners struggled. Do not confuse TARP with the Fed's emergency lending, which was separate.
example: Under the Capital Purchase Program, banks paid 5% a year on TARP preferred shares for the first five years and 9% after that. A bank that took, say, $10 billion owed $500 million a year at first, rising to $900 million from year six if it had not repaid.

short: A landmark Indian accounting fraud, revealed in January 2009, when Satyam Computer Services' founder admitted inventing over ₹5,000 crore of cash.
kid: The boss of a big company told everyone his piggy bank was full, but it was nearly empty and he had been pretending for years. When he finally told the truth, people were shocked and stopped trusting the company.
detail: On 7 January 2009, B. Ramalinga Raju, founder and chairman of Satyam Computer Services, then India's fourth-largest IT services firm, wrote to his board confessing that the accounts had been falsified for years. Of ₹5,361 crore of cash and bank balances in the books, ₹5,040 crore did not exist, and revenues and profits had been inflated too. The trigger was a failed December 2008 plan to buy two Raju family firms, Maytas Properties and Maytas Infra, which investors revolted against. The shares lost most of their value in a day. The government replaced the board, and Tech Mahindra won control of it in 2009. Auditors from PwC's Indian firms faced regulatory action, and the case shaped the Companies Act 2013's rules on independent directors, auditor rotation and fraud probes. The common confusion: the fraud hid not in complex products but in simple fake cash, which audits should have caught.
example: Satyam's books showed ₹5,361 crore of cash and bank balances, but ₹5,040 crore of it was fictitious. That is about 94% (5,040 / 5,361), leaving only about ₹321 crore that actually existed.

short: The 2009-2012 crisis in which Greece and other eurozone countries could no longer borrow affordably, needed bailouts and raised fears the euro would break up.
kid: A group of friends all shared the same kind of play tickets. One friend had borrowed far too much and could not pay back, and because they shared tickets, all the friends had to help or the group might fall apart.
detail: When the euro launched in 1999, weaker members such as Greece, Portugal and Spain could suddenly borrow almost as cheaply as Germany, and debts swelled. In late 2009 Greece revealed its budget deficit was far larger than reported, above 12% of GDP. Investors fled, bond yields of Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Italy (labelled the PIIGS) soared, and banks holding those bonds wobbled. Unable to devalue or print their own currency, Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Cyprus took EU-IMF bailouts tied to harsh austerity, and Spain got help for its banks. In 2012 private holders of Greek bonds took a large haircut. The turning point was ECB President Mario Draghi's July 2012 pledge to do whatever it takes to save the euro. The lesson: a shared currency without shared budgets leaves weak members exposed. PIIGS is now widely seen as a pejorative label.
example: In the March 2012 Greek debt exchange, private bondholders took a 53.5% cut in face value. An investor holding €1 million of Greek bonds received new Greek bonds and EFSF notes with a combined face value of €465,000 (1,000,000 × 46.5%), before counting further losses on their market value.

short: The 6 May 2010 plunge in which US stocks fell nearly 1,000 Dow points within minutes, then largely recovered: the best-known flash crash.
kid: One afternoon the sticker-swapping machines got confused and, for a few minutes, offered stickers for almost nothing. Then they calmed down and things went back to normal, but some people had already swapped at silly values.
detail: A flash crash is a sudden, deep fall in prices that reverses within minutes, usually because buyers vanish rather than because the news changes. The defining case came on 6 May 2010, amid worries about the Greek debt crisis. At about 2:32 pm New York time, a large fund began selling 75,000 E-mini S&P 500 futures contracts, worth about $4.1 billion, through an algorithm that sold quickly without regard to price. High-frequency traders passed contracts back and forth, liquidity evaporated, and the Dow sank to about 9% below its previous close before rebounding within about 20 minutes. Some shares briefly traded at a penny and others at $100,000. Regulators cancelled trades far from pre-crash prices and introduced single-stock circuit breakers and limit up-limit down bands. In 2015 a UK trader, Navinder Sarao, was charged with spoofing that contributed. The lesson: displayed liquidity can disappear exactly when it is needed.
example: The Dow closed at 10,868.12 on 5 May 2010 and fell as much as 998.5 points on 6 May, about 9.2% (998.5 / 10,868.12). Say a stop-loss on a hypothetical $50 stock was triggered and filled at $30: a $20 loss per share that stood, because only trades more than 60% away from pre-crash prices were cancelled.

short: The 2013 market sell-off, especially in emerging markets, after the US Fed hinted it would slow its bond buying, sending global borrowing costs sharply higher.
kid: A big helper had been handing out free sweets every month. When he just said he might hand out a few less someday, everyone panicked and rushed to grab theirs, even before anything changed.
detail: Under its third round of quantitative easing, the Fed was buying $85 billion of bonds a month. On 22 May 2013, Chair Ben Bernanke told Congress it could slow, or taper, those purchases within the next few meetings. Investors rushed to price in less support: the US 10-year Treasury yield rose from about 1.6% in early May to about 3% by September, and money fled emerging markets. Morgan Stanley labelled the hardest-hit economies, those with big current account deficits and reliance on foreign capital, the Fragile Five: Brazil, India, Indonesia, Turkey and South Africa. The rupee hit a record low near 68.8 per dollar in August 2013. The RBI tightened liquidity, curbed gold imports and, under new Governor Raghuram Rajan, opened an FCNR(B) deposit swap window that drew about $34 billion. Tapering was announced only in December 2013 and began in January 2014: the tantrum was about expectations.
example: The rupee went from about 55 per dollar in May 2013 to near 68.8 in late August. An Indian importer owing $1 million needed about ₹5.5 crore in May but about ₹6.88 crore in August, ₹1.38 crore more for the same bill.

short: The United Kingdom's exit from the European Union, chosen in a June 2016 referendum and completed in January 2020.
kid: A big club had many members who shared rules and played together freely. One member voted to leave, and then spent years working out new rules for how to still play with the others.
detail: On 23 June 2016, UK voters chose to leave the European Union by 51.9% to 48.1%. Markets had expected Remain, so the result shocked them: the pound suffered its biggest one-day fall in decades, global stocks slid, and the Bank of England cut its policy rate to a then-record low of 0.25% that August. The UK triggered Article 50 in March 2017, left on 31 January 2020 and exited the EU single market and customs union at the end of 2020, replacing them with a thinner trade agreement. For investors, Brexit meant years of political uncertainty, a weaker pound and pressure on UK-focused companies, while the FTSE 100's overseas earners gained from the cheaper currency. Indian firms with UK operations had to rethink their access to Europe. The common confusion: the UK never used the euro, so Brexit was about trade, laws and migration rules, not changing currency.
example: On referendum night the pound fell from about $1.50 to about $1.32 at its low, a drop of about 12% (0.18 / 1.50). A US investor's £1 million of UK shares, unchanged in pounds, went from about $1.5 million to about $1.32 million in dollar terms.
